lesson.text: Quick memory: what is empathy? (Imagining how someone else feels.) Empathy helps a lot when friends fall out.
Good friends are kind, fair and trustworthy. They listen, share and help. But even the best friends sometimes disagree, and that is normal.
A story: Zara and Bram both wanted to build a tower on the same spot. Zara grabbed the blocks; Bram shouted. Both felt cross.
Step 1: calm down. Take three slow breaths, or count to ten. It is hard to solve a problem while you are cross.
Step 2: talk and listen. Use I words: “I feel upset when you grab the blocks. I would like us to share.” Then listen to the other side without interrupting.
Step 3: find a win-win, an idea good for both. Zara and Bram built one taller tower together, with her design and his lanterns! Sometimes each gives a little: that is a compromise.
Step 4: make up. A real sorry says what you did and how you will put it right. Then forgive, and move on. If you cannot sort it out, ask a grown-up to help.
Try it in the world: plan a build with a friend. If you disagree, try the four steps: calm down, talk and listen, find a win-win, and make up.

exercises.prompt: What is the first step when friends fall out?
exercises.hint: It is hard to think clearly while you are cross.
exercises.explain: First calm down, with slow breaths or counting to ten.
True: disagreeing is normal. What matters is how friends sort it out.

exercises.prompt: Which is something a good friend does?
exercises.hint: What would you like a friend to do for you?
exercises.explain: Good friends listen, share and help.

exercises.prompt: It is easy to solve a problem while you are very cross.
exercises.hint: Why is calming down the first step?
exercises.explain: False: calm down first, then you can think and talk it through.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps for sorting out a falling-out in order.
exercises.hint: You cannot talk well until you are calm, and you make up at the end.
exercises.explain: Calm down, talk and listen, find a win-win, then make up.

exercises.hint: It starts with I and says how you feel.
choices: I feel sad when my tower is knocked down.
exercises.explain: “I feel sad when…” says how you feel without blaming, so the other person can listen.

choices: an idea that is good for both friends
exercises.explain: A win-win is a solution good for both, like Zara and Bram's tower.

exercises.prompt: Listening to the other side helps you understand the problem.
exercises.hint: Could your friend see things differently from you?
exercises.explain: True: listening shows you how your friend sees it.

exercises.prompt: Which is the best real sorry?
exercises.hint: A real sorry says what you did and how you will put it right.
choices: Sorry I took your blocks. I'll give them back.
Sorry, but it was your fault.
exercises.explain: Saying what you did and how you will fix it shows you mean it.

exercises.prompt: Tilly and Mimi both want the red blocks. What is a compromise?
exercises.hint: Each gives a little, so both get something.
choices: they each use half of the red blocks
exercises.explain: Sharing half each is a compromise: each gives a little and both are happy.

exercises.prompt: If you cannot sort out a problem together, it is fine to ask a grown-up for help.
exercises.explain: True: asking a trusted grown-up for help is a good idea when you are stuck.

exercises.prompt: After making up, what helps a friendship most?
exercises.hint: What helps both friends feel good again?
exercises.explain: Forgiving and moving on lets the friendship grow again.

exercises.prompt: Why does counting to ten help when you feel cross?
exercises.hint: What happens to your feelings when you wait a little?
choices: it gives your body time to calm down
it makes the other person leave
exercises.explain: Waiting while you count lets strong feelings settle, so you can think.

exercises.prompt: Match each step to what you do.
exercises.explain: Calm down with slow breaths, talk with I words and listen, find an idea good for both, then say a real sorry and forgive.

exercises.prompt: Sort the ways to talk: do they help, or hurt?
items: I feel upset when you grab.
exercises.hint: Does it say how you feel and what you would like, or does it blame?
exercises.explain: I words and kind questions help: I feel upset, can we take turns, I'd like us to share. Blaming or shutting someone out hurts: you always ruin it, go away, whatever.

exercises.prompt: Zara and Bram both wanted the same spot. Put what happened in order.
items: They built one tall tower together.
Zara grabbed the blocks and Bram shouted.
Each said how they felt and listened.
exercises.hint: Start with the falling-out, then follow the four steps.
exercises.explain: Zara grabbed and Bram shouted. Then they calmed down with slow breaths, each said how they felt and listened, and they found a win-win: one tall tower together.

exercises.prompt: Sort the ideas: a win-win, or one side wins?
exercises.hint: Is the idea good for both friends?
exercises.explain: Taking turns, building together and half each are good for both (half each is a compromise). Keeping every block, or letting the loudest decide, leaves one friend out.

exercises.prompt: Match each problem to a good next step.
matches: say sorry and give it back
exercises.hint: Think of the four steps, and of when to get help.
exercises.explain: Very cross: calm down first with slow breaths. Not knowing their side: listen without interrupting. Took a pen: a real sorry, and give it back. Stuck: ask a trusted grown-up to help.
